drawdown_context: HELE filed its FY25 10-K on 2025-04-24, only 21 days before the 2025-05-15 cutoff. FY25 (year ended Feb 28, 2025) was a year of meaningful deterioration: revenue -4.9% to $1,907.7M, operating income -45.2% to $142.7M, $51.5M Drybar impairment in Q4, and an explicit goodwill triggering event due to 'carrying value exceeding total enterprise value.' Diluted EPS fell 23.6% to $5.37. The 10-K subsequent-events section discloses the 145% China tariff effective 2025-04-09 and 125% Chinese retaliatory tariff effective 2025-04-11 -- HELE sources 63% of finished goods from China. The Olive & June acquisition closed 2024-12-16 for $229.4M cash + $15M contingent, funded by drawing the revolver. Total long-term debt rose to $916.9M (from $665.7M PY) with $887.5M maturing in fiscal 2029. Q4 fiscal-quarter buyback table shows Dec/Jan/Feb 2025 average prices of $69.19/$64.77/$58.39 -- sustained, severe decline. HELE was removed from the S&P 600 between 2025-05-15 and 2026-05-15.

rfm_tuples.R: 'During the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, we concluded a goodwill impairment triggering event had occurred due to a continued sustained decline in our stock price, resulting in our carrying value (excluding long-term debt) exceeding the Company total enterprise value (market capitalization plus long-term debt). Additional factors that contributed to this conclusion included downward revisions to our internal forecasts and strategic long-term plans... we recorded asset impairment charges of $51.5 million ($47.6 million after tax)... to reduce the goodwill and definite-lived trade name of our Drybar business.' (FY25 10-K, Note 7 + MD&A).
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A: confirm the impairment exists and quantify. Mode B: trace the triggering-event sequence across Q2 FY25 (test, no impairment) -> Q3 FY25 (no test) -> Q4 FY25 ($51.5M impairment) to detect 'kick-the-can' cadence and assess remaining at-risk goodwill/intangibles given the same factor (sustained stock decline) was true in Q2 but no impairment was recognized.
rfm_tuples.M_source: FY25 10-K Note 7 + Q3 FY25 10-Q (accession 0000916789-25-000004, filed 2025-01-08, period 2024-11-30) -- claim_evolution across the three impairment-event disclosures
rfm_tuples.M_value: SEQUENCE: (Q2 FY25) per Q3 10-Q -- 'During the second quarter of fiscal 2025, we concluded that a goodwill impairment triggering event had occurred primarily due to a sustained decline in our stock price,' performed quantitative testing on ALL reporting units and indefinite-lived intangibles; concluded NONE impaired. (Q3 FY25) per Q3 10-Q -- 'we determined no changes in circumstances or conditions or events have occurred that would indicate the carrying value of our goodwill and intangible assets may not be recoverable' -- declined to even retest despite the same depressed stock price and after closing the $229M Olive & June deal mid-quarter. (Q4 FY25) per FY25 10-K Note 7 -- took the $51.5M Drybar impairment, with management acknowledging 'downward revisions to our internal forecasts.' Remaining intangibles: goodwill $1,182.9M + indefinite trade names $358.2M + definite trade names $140.9M + trademark licenses $73.0M + customer relationships $47.3M = ~$1.80B (57% of $3.13B total assets). Q4 admission that 'carrying value (excluding long-term debt) exceeded total enterprise value' implies multiple non-Drybar reporting units are also below cover at cutoff.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding -- classic 'kicked-can' impairment cadence. Same factual condition (sustained stock decline below carrying value) was present in Q2 but produced no impairment; Q3 declined to retest; Q4 finally took only $51.5M against the smallest of three reporting units. The Q4 admission that consolidated carrying value > enterprise value mathematically implies more goodwill must come down, but management scoped the write-down narrowly. Forward path: additional impairments likely in Home & Outdoor and the rest of Beauty & Wellness within 2-4 quarters.

rfm_tuples.R: 'During fiscal 2025, we provided a qualified acquisition notice and, as a result, the maximum leverage ratio is 4.50 to 1.00 through November 30, 2025 and 3.50 to 1.00 thereafter... As of February 28, 2025, the amount available for revolving loans under the Credit Agreement was $312.4 million and the amount available per the maximum leverage ratio was $446.1 million.' (FY25 10-K Note 13 + MD&A Liquidity).
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A: confirm credit-agreement covenant-relief mechanic. Mode B: compute current leverage and headroom to the post-November 2025 step-down covenant of 3.50x. Cross-check against trailing EBITDA after the impairment and the rising-tariff cost path.
rfm_tuples.M_source: FY25 10-K Note 13 long-term debt schedule + MD&A Liquidity + balance sheet -- arithmetic
rfm_tuples.M_value: Total Credit Agreement borrowings $921.85M ($678.1M revolver + $243.75M term loan) at 2/28/25, vs $671.95M PY (+$250M YoY, primarily Olive & June funding). FY25 covenant EBITDA approximation = operating income $142.7M + D&A ~$50M + share-comp $21.4M + impairment add-back $51.5M + restructuring $14.8M + allowed addbacks = ~$305-325M; net debt $903M / mid-$315M = 2.87x. Filing itself notes covenants 'effectively limited our ability to incur more than $312.4M of additional debt' (headroom against the 4.50x cap is $312M; against the 3.50x cap that snaps back Dec 1, 2025 is roughly ~$10-100M). To stay compliant when covenant steps to 3.50x, HELE must (a) generate meaningful FCF to pay down $150-300M of debt by Nov 30, 2025, (b) grow EBITDA significantly while tariffs are RISING, or (c) seek another covenant amendment. The qualified-acquisition step-up is a ONE-TIME mechanism -- already used for Olive & June -- so HELE has no further programmatic relief available.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding -- critical pre-distress signal. HELE consumed its one-time qualified-acquisition covenant step-up to fund Olive & June at the same moment that (a) China tariffs jumped to 145% effective April 9, 2025, (b) US tariff exclusions expire in May 2025, (c) the company just took a $51.5M impairment indicating internal forecast cuts, and (d) the stock is well below 52-week highs limiting equity-financing options. The covenant snaps back to 3.50x Dec 1, 2025 -- just 6.5 months after cutoff. Even modest EBITDA degradation from tariff pass-through failure pushes HELE into amendment negotiation. Combined with $887M maturing in fiscal 2029, this is a clear 'covenant cliff + refi cliff' setup.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Sales to our largest customer, Amazon.com Inc., accounted for approximately 22%, 21% and 17% of our consolidated net sales revenue in fiscal 2025, 2024 and 2023, respectively. Sales to our second largest customer, Walmart, Inc., including its worldwide affiliates, accounted for approximately 11%, 9% and 10%... Sales to our third largest customer, Target Corporation, accounted for approximately 11% of our consolidated net sales revenue in fiscal 2025 and 10% in both fiscal 2024 and 2023... Sales to our top five customers accounted for approximately 49%, 47% and 43%...' (FY25 10-K Item 1, Customers).
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A: customer-concentration disclosure registry-confirmed. Mode B: rising concentration trajectory (43% -> 47% -> 49% top-5; Amazon 17% -> 21% -> 22%) is itself an Underdelivery signal -- management is increasingly dependent on three retailers that are private-label predators and on Amazon algorithmic merchandising, exactly when 145% tariffs make pass-through pricing power load-bearing.
rfm_tuples.M_source: FY25 10-K + FY24 10-K + FY23 10-K customer-concentration disclosures -- trajectory analysis
rfm_tuples.M_value: Top-5 customer concentration rose 6 points in 2 years (43% -> 49%). Amazon alone moved 17% -> 21% -> 22% -- a 5-point rise, ~$95M of incremental Amazon dependency on a $1.91B revenue base. The risk-factor section warns: 'as large traditional retail and online customers grow even larger and become more sophisticated, they may continue to demand lower pricing, special packaging, shorter lead times... use of private label brands.' HELE Hydro Flask competes directly with Stanley/Yeti/Owala on Amazon; OXO competes with Amazon Basics; Vicks/Honeywell/Braun in Wellness face private-label encroachment. The 145% China tariff hits hardest on the high-volume, low-margin, private-label-vulnerable categories.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding: increasing customer concentration during a period of tariff escalation is doubly bad -- Amazon/Walmart/Target have buyer-power leverage to refuse price increases needed to pass through 145% tariffs. The risk-factor language is generic boilerplate but the trajectory (Amazon +5pts in 2y) is not flagged in MD&A. Mode B: 'if concentration is rising and tariffs are rising, what is the FY26 gross-margin path?' The filing does not quantify the tariff pass-through assumption, which is the load-bearing question for the next 4-6 quarters.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Finished goods manufactured by vendors in China comprised approximately 63%, 62% and 73% of finished goods purchased in fiscal 2025, 2024 and 2023, respectively... As of April 9, 2025, the U.S. has imposed an aggregate additional 145% tariff on imports from China... China announced a reciprocal 125% tariff on imports from the U.S. effective April 11, 2025... we obtained exclusions from tariffs imposed in fiscal years 2019 and 2020 from the USTR on certain products... These exclusions expire in May 2025 which will result in higher tariffs assessed on the related products.' (FY25 10-K Risk Factors + MD&A).
rfm_tuples.f: Mode B: estimate the FY26 tariff cost exposure given the 63% China sourcing mix and 145% incremental rate; check whether management quantifies the exposure or commits to specific mitigation; note that USTR exclusions expire the SAME MONTH AS CUTOFF.
rfm_tuples.M_source: FY25 10-K Risk Factors + MD&A 'Inflation and Tariff' discussion
rfm_tuples.M_value: Exposure math: FY25 COGS = $993.3M. China-sourced finished goods ~63% of finished goods purchased = ~$540-625M of landed cost (finished goods are most of COGS). Marginal 145% incremental tariff on that landed-input value would represent multi-hundred-million-dollar annual gross cost if no mitigation -- several multiples of FY25 operating income of $142.7M. Even partial mitigation (sourcing diversification, supplier negotiation, price increases) leaves a highly material FY26 hit. The filing explicitly states: 'We are in the process of determining our incremental tariff cost exposure in light of continuing changes to tariff policies, and the full extent of our potential mitigation plans, as well as the associated timing to implement such plans.' Management refused to provide FY26 guidance, did not affirm or withdraw any prior outlook, and did not quantify tariff impact. The pre-2019 USTR exclusions expire in May 2025 -- the cutoff month -- adding incremental cost on products previously exempt.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding: the FY25 10-K describes the 145% China tariff as a known fact (effective 2 weeks before filing) yet provides no FY26 quantification and no FY26 outlook. This is a deliberate disclosure choice: management knows the math but chose not to commit. The framework reading: tariff-induced gross-margin compression on top of an already-declining revenue base (organic -5.9% FY25), a leveraged balance sheet (~2.9x EBITDA snapping to 3.50x covenant Dec 1 2025), customer concentration limiting pass-through pricing power, and USTR exclusions expiring in May 2025 -- all together imply severe FY26 EBITDA compression that the filing does not acknowledge. Refusing FY26 guidance in April 2025 is itself the tell.

rfm_tuples.R: 'In August 2024, our Board of Directors authorized the repurchase of up to $500 million of our outstanding common stock... As of February 28, 2025, our repurchase authorization allowed for the purchase of $499.9 million of common stock.' (FY25 10-K Note 10). Open-market repurchases FY25: 1,011,243 shares for $100.0M at average $98.91. Q4 FY25 Issuer Purchases table shows December avg $69.19, January $64.77, February $58.39 -- only de-minimis shares tendered for tax withholding; 'For the periods presented, there were no common stock open market repurchases.'
rfm_tuples.f: Mode B: capital-allocation asymmetry. Did HELE buy back when expensive and stop when cheap? Does the timing of the buyback authorization expansion (Aug 2024) coincide with the Olive & June negotiation, telegraphing internal capital-deployment competition?
rfm_tuples.M_source: FY25 10-K Note 10 + Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities table + cash-flow statement; FY24 10-K comp
rfm_tuples.M_value: FY25 open-market buybacks: 1,011,243 shares at avg $98.91 = $100M. FY24 open-market buybacks: 381,200 shares at avg $131.18 = $50M. HELE doubled buyback dollars in FY25 at an average price 70% above the Feb 2025 closing-month avg ($58.39). Q4 FY25 (Dec-Feb): ZERO open-market buybacks despite a brand-new $500M authorization with $499.9M unused. Pattern: heavy buying at $99-131 avg, no buying at $58-69. Simultaneously, FY25 cash to Olive & June ($229.4M + $15M contingent) drained financial flexibility that would have funded buybacks at the trough. Classic asymmetric capital-allocation tell: deployed at high valuations, withheld at low valuations.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding -- strong forensic signal. HELE bought $100M of stock at $98.91 in FY25 while management's own Q4 impairment language admits the carrying value exceeded total enterprise value. They either (a) overpaid for buybacks on a value-destructive basis with knowledge they were doing so, or (b) genuinely thought shares were undervalued at $99 -- in which case the absence of buybacks at $58-69 in Q4 is a covenant/liquidity-constraint reveal (HELE no longer had balance-sheet capacity given Olive & June + revolver draw). Either reading is bearish. The $499.9M unused 'theater authorization' announced August 2024 cannot be executed against by Q4 2025.

rfm_tuples.R: 'On December 16, 2024, we completed the acquisition of Olive & June, LLC... The total purchase consideration consists of initial cash consideration of $229.4 million, net of cash acquired... and contingent cash consideration of up to $15.0 million subject to Olive & June performance during calendar years 2025, 2026, and 2027... The acquisition... advances our Elevate for Growth Strategy to deploy accretive capital that leverages our capabilities and scale to accelerate growth, further expand margins, and drive greater earnings growth and free cash flow conversion.' (FY25 10-K Note 6). Goodwill recorded: $154.8M (67.5% of purchase price). 'Olive & June sales... approximately eleven weeks of operating results' contributed $23.0M.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode B: implied annual run-rate, implied revenue multiple, and consistency of 'accretive' claim with timing (acquired at peak of consumer M&A cycle weeks before tariff escalation; goodwill 67.5% of purchase price is high; immediately followed by Q4 impairment of a different B&W brand acquired in the prior wave).
rfm_tuples.M_source: FY25 10-K Note 6 (Acquisitions) + Note 7 (Goodwill rollforward) + MD&A Liquidity
rfm_tuples.M_value: Olive & June implied run-rate: $23.0M from 11 weeks = ~$109M annualized. Purchase price $229.4M = 2.1x revenue. Goodwill $154.8M of $229.4M = 67.5% -- high goodwill fraction signals limited tangible/identifiable-IP justification. The deal closed Dec 16 2024 -- weeks before the Trump tariff escalation. Nail-care products (manicure systems, polish, press-ons, tools) are largely manufactured offshore (China is the dominant nail-tool source) so the acquired business carries direct 145% tariff exposure. Within 75 days of closing, HELE took a $51.5M impairment on Drybar (a comparable Beauty & Wellness prestige acquisition from 2019), with management acknowledging downward forecast revisions. Contingent $15M payment cap over 3 years suggests sellers got a muted earn-out (limited future-performance conviction at the closing price).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding: the timing/sequencing of Olive & June is the strongest capital-allocation tell. Management used the one-time qualified-acquisition covenant step-up to close at the top of the tariff-policy uncertainty window, then within 90 days took a $51.5M Drybar impairment on a comparable prior Beauty acquisition. The 'accretive capital' claim is stated in present tense in the 10-K -- not registered as a forecast or risk. Mode B: 'if Drybar is impaired and management revised internal forecasts down, why is Olive & June $154.8M goodwill assumed intact?' Bayesian read: forward 12-24 month base-rate probability of Olive & June goodwill impairment is elevated.

PCAOB ID 248. No going-concern language; clean unqualified opinion. Critical Audit Matters: (1) Goodwill impairment assessment -- Drybar reporting unit; (2) Trade name impairment assessment -- Drybar.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A: auditor_change_tracker, going_concern_detector. Mode B: tier-2 auditor at a $1.9B-revenue NASDAQ company with $1.8B of intangibles is a yellow flag; 18-year continuous tenure raises audit-independence questions; CAM scoping confined to a single reporting unit ignores broader carrying-value-vs-enterprise-value disclosure.
rfm_tuples.M_source: FY25 10-K auditor opinion + 5y lookback Item 4.01 search through 2025-05-15 cutoff
rfm_tuples.M_value: Auditor: Grant Thornton (NOT Big 4). 18-year continuous tenure (2007-2025). Critical Audit Matters confined to the Drybar impairment that was already booked -- i.e., the auditor did NOT escalate goodwill on the rest of the portfolio (Olive & June, OXO/Home & Outdoor, Hydro Flask, Osprey, Honeywell-licensed, Hot Tools, Curlsmith, etc.) to CAM despite the explicit 'carrying value > enterprise value' triggering language. No 8-K Item 4.01 filings pre-cutoff. No qualifications, no going concern.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding: tier-2 audit firm + 18-year tenure + tight Critical Audit Matter scope (only Drybar, the smallest reporting unit) at a company that just disclosed enterprise-value-below-carrying-value. The auditor framing is 'one reporting unit impaired, others fine' but management own triggering-event language admits a broader consolidated carrying-value problem. A Big 4 auditor would more likely have escalated multiple reporting units to CAM. The clean going-concern (no GC language) is calibrated correctly given HELE is not at imminent failure -- hence MODERATE_UNDERDELIVERY rather than RED_FLAG: incomplete disclosure of impairment scope rather than financial-distress concealment.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Our Drybar business has continued to experience a decline in net sales revenue due to lower consumer demand, increased competition, and net distribution declines, all of which have contributed to reduced earnings and cash flows. In connection with our annual budgeting and forecasting process, management reduced its forecasts of Drybar net sales revenue growth, gross margin and earnings before interest and taxes which also resulted in management selecting a lower royalty rate.' (FY25 10-K Note 7). Beauty & Wellness segment FY25 sales -8.0% (-10.0% organic).
rfm_tuples.f: Mode B: claim_evolution -- the Beauty & Wellness 'softer consumer demand, increased competition, net distribution declines' factors named for Drybar are the same factors causing the segment-wide -10.0% organic decline. If those factors caused $51.5M impairment of one brand, what is the at-risk goodwill in the rest of Beauty & Wellness ($691M post-impairment)?
rfm_tuples.M_value: Beauty & Wellness FY25 organic -10.0%, segment operating margin collapsed from 10.8% (FY24) to 2.3% (FY25) GAAP. Drybar impairment factors (consumer demand decline, competition, distribution declines) match the segment-wide drivers. Q3 FY25 (3 months ended 2024-11-30): B&W organic -9.3%; YTD organic -10.6%. Q3 also flagged 'shipping disruption from Curlsmith system integration challenges' -- i.e., Curlsmith integration is still problematic 3 years post-acquisition (acquired April 2022 for ~$165M). Hot Tools (acquired 2010), Drybar (2019), Curlsmith (2022) are all prestige-hair brands suffering the same demand pattern; Olive & June (2024) is now in the same segment.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding: the auditor scoped the impairment to Drybar only, but management own narrative attributes the same causes to the entire Beauty & Wellness segment. If lower consumer demand + increased competition + distribution declines justified writing down Drybar carrying value by $51.5M (goodwill to $134.3M, trade name to $7.0M), the same factors should be flagged against Curlsmith, Hot Tools, and prestige-hair-adjacent brands. The narrow scoping is consistent with management protecting reported goodwill in a quarter when stock-price weakness already threatened consolidated covenant compliance. Future B&W impairments are highly probable.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Our current policy is to retain earnings to provide funds for the operation and expansion of our business, common stock repurchases and for potential acquisitions. We have not paid any cash dividends on our common stock since inception.' (FY25 10-K Item 5).
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A: confirm dividend policy. Mode B: with no dividend and buybacks halted in Q4, there is no current capital-return-to-shareholders mechanism. Combined with cash deployment to Olive & June and the upcoming covenant step-down, the equity holder is effectively subordinated to debt repair and acquisition integration for the foreseeable future.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Zero dividend, never paid since inception. Buybacks: $100M FY25 at avg $98.91 (essentially all before stock collapse). Cash balance at FYE: only $18.9M (down from $18.5M PY -- essentially zero net cash). Long-term debt $916.9M against stockholders equity $1,683M. The only equity-return mechanism (buybacks) requires both balance-sheet capacity AND covenant compliance -- both constrained. The $500M buyback authorization is functionally unused ($499.9M remaining).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding: shareholders have no near-term return mechanism. No dividend. Buybacks effectively suspended (Q4 zero open-market activity despite $500M authorization). Cash deployed to Olive & June at top of tariff cycle. Net debt rising. The equity bull case requires either (a) re-rating from multiple expansion (unlikely with tariff-compressed margins and covenant cliff) or (b) earnings growth (contradicted by FY25 organic -5.9% and tariff headwinds). The 'theater authorization' of $500M unused buyback is bearish window-dressing.

rfm_tuples.R: Mode B: M&A track record on Beauty & Wellness. HELE acquired Drybar (April 2019, ~$255M), Curlsmith (April 2022, ~$165M), Olive & June (December 2024, $229.4M + $15M contingent). FY25 net sales of Beauty & Wellness $1.0B (organic -10.0%); GAAP operating margin 2.3%; segment took $51.5M Drybar impairment and Q3 10-Q flagged 'Curlsmith system integration challenges' shipping disruption.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode B: serial-acquirer-with-recurring-impairment pattern. If Drybar impaired in Year 6 post-acquisition, and Curlsmith is having integration issues in Year 3, then Olive & June is on a high-base-rate impairment path within 3-4 years.

rfm_tuples.M_value: Drybar bought 2019 for ~$255M -> impaired $51.5M (~20% of original price) in 2025 = 6yr post-deal write-down. Curlsmith bought 2022 for ~$165M -> 'shipping disruption from Curlsmith system integration challenges' explicitly cited in FY25 10-K MD&A and Q3 FY25 10-Q = 3yr post-deal still integrating. Project Pegasus (initiated FY23) has $14.8M FY25 restructuring charges + $7.7M remaining liability -- the company is in continuous restructuring mode while still adding acquisitions. Olive & June (Dec 2024) is now in the same B&W pipeline. The 'Elevate for Growth Strategy' explicitly relies on continued accretive M&A.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B finding: pattern-of-failure across the Beauty & Wellness M&A program. The 'Elevate for Growth' narrative requires accretive acquisitions producing margin expansion; the actual track record shows ongoing restructuring and Drybar impairment. The narrative claim 'deploy accretive capital that leverages our capabilities and scale' is contradicted by every concurrent disclosure: organic -10.0% B&W, impaired Drybar, struggling Curlsmith integration, and tariff overhang that hits Beauty import-heavy COGS structure hardest. Forward base-rate for additional B&W goodwill impairment is elevated.

summary: At 2025-05-15, HELE shows multiple stacked Mode B distress signals despite clean deterministic flags (no going concern, no auditor change, Grant Thornton continuous since 2007). The strongest signals: (1) IMPAIRMENT KICK-THE-CAN -- Q2 FY25 triggering event + quantitative test = no impairment; Q3 = no test; Q4 = $51.5M Drybar impairment with admission 'carrying value > enterprise value' (i.e., other reporting units are also under cover and likely to be written down). (2) COVENANT CLIFF -- used one-time qualified-acquisition step-up (3.50 -> 4.50x leverage) to fund Olive & June; snaps back to 3.50x on Dec 1, 2025 with only ~$70-100M of EBITDA headroom against RISING tariff costs. (3) TARIFF MATH -- 63% China sourcing exposed to 145% incremental tariffs effective 2025-04-09, USTR exclusions expire May 2025 (cutoff month), and management refuses to quantify FY26 impact or give guidance. (4) BUYBACK ASYMMETRY -- bought $100M at avg $98.91 in FY25, zero open-market in Q4 when stock hit $58.39, $499.9M authorization unused = theater authorization lacking execution capacity. (5) OLIVE & JUNE TIMING -- acquired at $229.4M (67.5% goodwill ratio) weeks before tariff escalation, while a comparable B&W brand (Drybar) was being impaired and Curlsmith integration is still failing 3 years post-deal. KEY ANSWER: yes, the framework would have flagged HELE one year earlier; the combination of impairment-cadence underdelivery + covenant-cliff math + unquantified tariff exposure + asymmetric capital allocation + serial-acquirer-impairment-pattern is detectable from the FY25 10-K alone. Deterministic-only screens (auditor change, going concern) would have missed.
